title: Create your hero
description: Give the adventure a hero and a useful tool.

tasks.title: Remember a detail with a variable
tasks.body: A variable is a name that refers to a value. Write hero = "Nova" to store a name. Later, use hero without quotes to read the value.
tasks.detail: The equals sign assigns a value; it does not print anything. print("hero") displays the word hero. print(hero) displays the value stored under that name. Define a variable before you use it.

tasks.note: Changing the two assignments updates the character details without changing the print instructions.

tasks.question: What does print(hero) display after hero = "Nova"?
tasks.why: Without quotes, hero means “use the value stored in this variable.” That value is the string Nova.

tasks.prompt: Change Nova to your hero’s name and lantern to a tool of your choice. Run the code to see both values.
Store a nonempty hero name in hero and a nonempty tool in tool. Print both values by using the variables. You may add labels or combine them into a sentence.
tasks.starter:
hero = ""
tool = ""
# Print hero and tool, using the variables
hints: This card needs two variables, hero and tool, each holding some text. Then print() shows them.
Look at the first two lines: put your own words between the empty quotes. Then check your print(): a variable name goes inside it with no quotes.
With other names: pet = "___" stores text, and print(pet) shows it. Do the same with hero and tool.

error_hints.text: Names must be spelled exactly the same each time: hero in print() must match hero where you gave it a value, letter for letter.
Text values need matching quotes, like "Kai". Variable names inside print() do not.
If your output shows the words hero and tool instead of your values, remove the quotes around the names inside print().

similar_example.code:
pet = "Biscuit"
bed = "rug"
print(pet + " sleeps on the " + bed)
similar_example.note: Two variables hold text, and print() shows their values by name. Your challenge does the same with hero and tool.

other_ways.note: An f-string puts the values straight into the sentence.
print() can take several values separated by commas, and puts a space between them.

messages.message: Assign nonempty text to hero and tool, then print their values using the variables. Quoted "hero" prints the word, not its stored value.
hero and tool both hold text, and your program prints their values by using the variables. Change one value and run again: does your story change the way you expect?
